item.title: Product Leadership in Robotics: A Framework for Structural Commercialization (Learn over Earn)
item.content:encoded:
Build great tech. Sell aggressively.

That sequence works in software. In robotics and deep tech, it systematically fails.

I have seen this pattern repeatedly, both as an operator and as an investor. Strong engineering teams. Genuine technical breakthroughs. Often thoughtful product direction. Then commercial pressure arrives too early, and the system destabilizes. Recovery is hard and painful, sometimes unachievable..

At the same time, some companies recognize the issue early and take a different path. In my work with founders, executives, and product and R&D leaders, and through board-level involvement as an investor, I see how differently these companies approach growth.

The difference is structural. Robotics companies do not fail because they cannot sell. They fail because they commercialize in the wrong sequence.

This requires a different model. I call it Structural Commercialization.

The Two Types of Commercialization (and Why Conflating Them Is Dangerous)

Most companies treat commercialization as a single activity. It is not. There are two fundamentally different modes, and confusing them creates predictable failure.

Performative commercialization is what companies optimize for externally. Revenue targets, pipeline growth, signed contracts, and metrics that signal traction to investors and boards. This is necessary. It is also the end state.

Structural commercialization comes before that. Its purpose is not to maximize revenue, but to ensure the product can reliably create value under real-world conditions.

Insights are your currency.

In this phase, commercial activity is not driven by scale, but by learning. Every pilot, every deployment, every customer interaction is designed to test specific assumptions about the system: technical performance, operational constraints, integration requirements, and economic viability.

Revenue can occur, but it is not the objective. The objective is to remove uncertainty from the product until value delivery becomes predictable. Without this phase, revenue is unstable by definition.

Where Companies Go Wrong?

Most robotics companies operate with partial understanding of a highly complex system, while believing they understand enough to scale. This includes the belief that they are strong at product leadership, when often the opposite is true.

They know they need pilots, but treat them as early sales rather than structured experiments. They deploy systems without clearly defined learning objectives. They expect insights to emerge passively instead of designing mechanisms to extract them. Companies know they need revenue, so they "commercialize" before the product can consistently deliver value.

Now, think about what can happen (and often does happen) when a robotics company attempts performative commercialization too early:

  • A Sales team team is hired too early.
  • The product isn't reliable enough. Failures appear in real-world use. Learning mechanisms aren't established as inA customer-facing layer is introduced to handle those failures. Engineering is pulled into reactive work. Resources shift from resolving fundamental issues to managing symptoms.
  • At the same time, the cost structure expands. Sales and customer functions consume capital that would be required to complete the product.
  • Conflicting pressures emerge. Sales pushes for commitments. Engineering needs time and/or more resources to close reliability gaps.
  • Leadership bandwidth is consumed by crisis management.
  • The underlying issues remain unresolved or are resolved slowly with high resource burn.

Meanwhile, each additional customer increases the surface area of the problem. The system does not scale. The instability does. You are not scaling a product. You are scaling unresolved complexity.

This isn't theory. I have lived it. I see robotics companies on this exact path everywhere.

There is a better path. I see successful robotics companies following it.

The result is predictable. Sales teams are hired too early. R&D is pushed to meet external commitments instead of resolving core uncertainties. Pilots accumulate without increasing understanding. Focus is placed on optimizing the product roadmap instead of meaningfully re-visiting the company strategy and plan. Complexity compounds faster than the organization can absorb it.

At that point, pressure increases across the system. Sales is told to push harder. Engineering is told to deliver faster. Neither can resolve the underlying issue.

This is not a sales problem. It is not an R&D problem. It is a sequencing problem at the level of company leadership.

Figure 1: Transition away from an oversimplified model to commercialize prematurely. Recognize that commercialization should be structured differently for robotics and embrace a phase of Structural Commercialization.

The Four States of a Robotics Product Journey

Deep tech products move through distinct states. Each state requires different mechanisms, different leadership, and different expectations.

Most software companies operate as if the journey is: Build → Ship → Sell → Scale.

In robotics and deep tech that model breaks. The journey is more intense, often longer (but not always), and less forgiving:

State 1: Fundamental Innovation

The system must make something possible that was not possible before. Not an incremental improvement, but a breakthrough. This is pure R&D. There is no product yet, only the emergence of one. Commercial pressure at this stage is counterproductive. It distorts priorities before the technical foundation exists.

State 2: Product Completion to Performance Threshold

The core breakthrough exists, or is clearly within reach. The problem now is not invention, but reliability. The system must be pushed to a point where it can consistently deliver value under real-world conditions. That threshold is non-negotiable.

This is where Structural Commercialization lives. You're learning, not selling. with the market as your laboratory. Insights are your currency. The key question is precise: what must be true for this product to perform reliably enough to create value?

State 3: Value Creation Unlocked

Something shifts when you cross the performance threshold. Think: 99% vs 99.9% reliability. This can be the difference between a robot that falls down stairs once a week (breaks before it creates real product value) and one that never falls (actual product). Value is binary in robotics. Almost-good-enough has no business model in deep tech. The full value is only created when the solution is verifiably complete.

State 4: Functioning Business Model

Only here does performative commercialization make sense. The product works. Customers can depend on it. Now you build a sales organization, set commercial targets, and scale. In practice, elements of sales should begin forming toward the end of State 3, when reliable value delivery is within measurable reach. Not earlier (i.e. not when founder and investor pressure demand more sales).

The critical mistake is collapsing State 2 and State 4 into one. They look similar on the surface, but they operate on entirely different logics.

They require different people, different metrics, different investor expectations, and a different mindset.

For this reason, embedding product leadership early into a company is key. Leadership through a product lens must drive the company through the first three states.

Why Complexity Changes Everything (Especially in Robotics)

Software operates in a relatively contained environment. Code is written, deployed, observed, and corrected. In comparison to robotics, feedback loops are tight and inexpensive. Failures are usually recoverable.

Deep tech operates across multiple tightly coupled layers: hardware, software, manufacturing, certification, and deployment in unstructured environments. Each layer introduces constraints. Their interaction multiplies complexity.

On top of that, robotics still requires finding solutions to multiple unresolved technical frontiers. These breakthroughs add an extra layer of complexity, which in robotics includes (but isn’t limited to):

  • Understanding surroundings
  • High-level reasoning & planning
  • Truly reliable learning transfer
  • Complex (mobile) Manipulation
  • Dexterous hands & tactile sensing

These are not integration problems. They are open problems.

This leads to a fundamental hypothesis I've come to believe deeply, from years of experience:

Developing a complex product (like a robot) increases the risk of becoming a complex company.

Once that happens, organizational energy goes toward managing complexity rather than eliminating it.

Figure 2: In deep tech, product complexity and company complexity are strongly interlinked. In robotics, the current need for breakthroughs is an additional complexity layer.

Product Leadership as a Solution

If enabled and given agency, strong product leaders recognize this spiral early and actively work to kill product complexity, thus also killing potential company complexity. Product leadership keeps the organization focused on product completion. They know that breakthroughs that don’t arrive on cue.

Ideally, product leadership and company leadership work hand-in-hand to:

  • resist premature expansion of company functions
  • resist prematurely chasing earnings.

All ensure that energy flows toward development, not away from it. This increased focus increases the probability of achieving breakthroughs. This is the discipline that separates companies that scale from companies that stall.

What Structural Commercialization Actually Looks Like

If structural commercialization isn't sales, what is it?

  • It's founder or product-led partner-oriented business development with structured learning objectives.
  • It’s the design and execution of a conscious interaction between your company, your product, and your core market
  • It's an investment to ultimately more sustainable commercialization

Here is what it looks like in practice:

Partner-customers, not paying customers. In structural commercialization, you're looking for customers who share your learning goals, not customers who simply want your product to work. These are different people. A partner-customer understands they're participating in product development and values that participation. They provide investment in the form of some financial support, access, feedback, and real-world data. They don't expect the product to be finished.

Hypothesis-based pilots. Every pilot has an explicit learning question: What are we testing? What outcome confirms our hypothesis? What would refute it? Without this structure, pilots generate anecdotes, not insights. And anecdotes can't feed a product requirements process.

Think: "Does the robot navigate reliably on wet surfaces in a food processing environment?" is a testable hypothesis. "Let's deploy and see how it goes" is not.

Insights flow directly to product requirements. The learning loop must be tight. Insights from structural commercialization go directly into requirements, then are tested against them, and pass through product leadership for prioritization. This is why structural commercialization should be product-led or founder-led, not sales-led. The commercial activity is a direct input to the product, not a measure of it.

Figure 3: A concentrated learning loop in the "learn over earn" phase of structural commercialization.

Resist building a sales organization for as long as reasonable. This is the hardest discipline. Investors ask about sales. Boards ask about pipeline. But a premature sales organization creates its own gravity and it pulls the company toward promises the product can't yet keep. Sales people are incentivized to sell, even when selling is the wrong move. Product leaders are motivated by product completion and value creation, the exact outputs of the structural commercialization phase.

The Learning Phases in Practice: An Example by Batch Sizes and Verification

Build 2 "similar" robots, then 5 "similar," then 10 "the same," then hundreds of "identical" robots

Structural commercialization isn't one phase. It's a progression. One practical way to think about it is in batch sizes. I am currently working this way with one robotics company in an overarching picture that connects batches, learning goals, learning mechanisms with future funding, key hires, and core financial planning.

Batch 1: First 3-10 units — Engineer Self-Verification

In the earliest deployments, engineers are building and verifying their own work. The batch is small enough that the people who designed the system are also the ones deploying it, observing it, and learning from it. The learning goals at this stage are fundamental: Does the core technology work outside the lab? What breaks first? What assumptions were wrong? What must change in the system design before we freeze it?

Self-verification is fine here and often necessary. Nobody else understands the system well enough to verify it yet. But product leaders must be intentional about what this batch is for. Even if labelled a pilot or customer deployment, its true nature is structured learning with specific requirements in focus and clear criteria for what "good enough to move to the next batch" looks like.

Batch 2: Next deployment wave — Beyond Self-Verification

This is where many companies fail to evolve. Based on what you learned from Batch 1, the next wave must consciously introduce new mechanisms, ideally moving beyond engineer self-verification. Why? Because self-verification has a blind spot: the people who designed the system are the least likely to challenge their own assumptions. Designs that should be evolving can become static too early when the same engineers are both building and judging. Especially if those engineers lack outside-in insights.

In this phase, engineering and product leaders should introduce independent verification: a different entity (e.g. whether an internal test/verification team, a partner customer's operations team, or an external validation partner) that challenges the system designs from a fresh perspective. This is also where industrial engineering should enter the picture, at latest overlapping with the tail end of the design phase. The goal is to ensure that insights from real-world deployment feed back into requirements before any hardware system design is frozen.

In short, it helps everyone realize if their "baby is ugly" before it's too late.

This overlap is critical and often missed. If your learning loop from deployment doesn't reach back into active design work and if the design is already locked when field insights arrive, you've lost one of the most valuable feedback channels structural commercialization provides.

Batch 3 and beyond: Converging on the performance threshold

Each subsequent batch should have progressively sharper learning objectives, tighter verification, and clearer evidence that the product is converging toward "boringly reliable." The metrics should show that open issues are shrinking, not expanding. When the data shows convergence, not when founder or investor pressure demands it, is when you begin the transition to performative commercialization.

A Manufacturing Quest

There's a parallel progression that must happen alongside the learning batches: manufacturing maturity. Having scalable manufacturing in mind from the beginning helps anticipate long-term sourcing, production capacity, and quality control during assembly.

If you cannot build 1-3 prototype robots “somehow”, then 5 "similar," then 10 "the same," then hundreds of "identical" robots, your solution won't be scalable, will probably be unreliable, and will be uncertifiable. The progression from engineering workshop to professional manufacturing is itself a company challenge, and it must overlap with the learning phases, not follow them.

The European Dimension

Currently, European robotics companies have a smaller margin for error. Full stop.

Less funding. Smaller domestic markets. A talent pool that, while exceptional in many respects, is distributed across a continent with different languages, regulatory environments, and cultural norms around risk-taking. 31 of 42 Swiss startup exits in 2025 went to international buyers (then Rivr was sold to Amazon in early 2026), often because scaling capital wasn't available domestically or the founders preferred a life-changing moment over the challenge of building a global company, based in Europe.

Europe's best robotics companies are either young or haven't been built yet.

In the US, large funding can buy margin for error. A company can make the mistake of premature commercialization and survive it with enough capital to course-correct. In Europe, that luxury rarely exists. The errors compound:

  • Underestimate development timelines (common, because deep tech is harder than expected)
  • Attempt to generate revenue before the product is ready (to satisfy investors and extend runway)
  • Underinvest in the actual adoption work required after the product is complete
  • Run multiple products in parallel to spread commercial risk (which actually multiplies complexity)

Each of these individually is damaging. Together, they're catastrophic. And they're far more common in European robotics companies than they should be.

Figure 4: Mistakes made in robotics companies compound in a spiral of complexity.

My optimistic view: Europe's best robotics companies are either young or haven't been built yet. The ones that will succeed will be product-led, not sales-led. They will master structural commercialization before they attempt performative commercialization. They will resist the pressure to "sell like hell" until they have something worth selling.

This is why product leadership may be the single most undervalued role in European deep tech. The companies that get this right will have product leaders (or founders who think like product leaders) at the strategic center of the company, not as a support function. Their chances of winning are vastly increased with the right investors ;)

The Investor Dimension

You cannot do this alone. Structural commercialization requires investors who believe in the learn-over-earn philosophy. Not all investors do or even realize that it should exist.

Some investors pressure companies to show commercial traction before the product is ready. This pressure is understandable from a portfolio management perspective. Investors need data points, they need signals, they need to be able to defend the investment to their LPs. But this pressure, applied at the wrong phase, is one of the most reliable ways to damage and early robotics company.

The right founder-investor conversation sounds like this: "The product isn’t ready and that’s fine for this phase. We are in structural commercialization. Here is what we're learning. Here is how that learning is accelerating our path to the performance threshold. Here are the specific hypotheses we've validated in the last quarter. Here is what we expect to learn in the next one."

That is a meaningful progress report. It's just not one that fits neatly into a "revenue this quarter" slide.

Finding investors who understand this distinction, and who have the patience to support the learn-over-earn phase, is itself a strategic task. It's part of building the right company. An investor who pushes you into premature performative commercialization is not a neutral actor. They are a risk to your roadmap and company.

Figure 5: A supportive deep tech investor.

I am fortunate to have a dual voice as an investor and company builder, giving me the combined knowledge from the wider ecosystem and the deep knowledge of company and product development. I used that combined knowledge to help our portfolio companies buffer investor / board input and stay in structural commercialization until a boringly reliable product is clearly within sight.

When is that? Quantitatively, the right 2-3 metrics will make that clear. Qualitatively, when your customer is no longer excited that the robot completed the task, when it's expected, unremarkable, routine, then you're approaching the threshold.

What Happens When You Get It Right

The path through structural commercialization can feel slower in the early phases and is excitingly much faster in the later ones.

A company that masters structural commercialization arrives at State 4: Functioning Business Model with something precious: a product that works and creates clear value, a set of partner customers who are advocates rather than passive voices or detractors, and a clear understanding of which market segments the product serves reliably.

That's a foundation. Sales now has something real to sell. The customer success function supports growth rather than managing damage. Engineering can focus on the next capability rather than closing reliability gaps in the last one. The business model is legible.

The commercial velocity in State 4, for a company that achieved State 2: Product Completion to Performance Threshold well, is genuinely faster than for a company that tried to skip ahead. The short-term delay in structural commercialization is paid back with interest.

Think:

  • Waymo. Sixteen years to offer reliable rides from the San Francisco airport. Excruciatingly slow by Silicon Valley standards. But now? They're expanding. And the reliability foundation they built is not easily replicated by competitors who tried to move faster.
  • Ascento. This is a Zurich-based robotics company who stayed lean and focused. They prioritized learning, stabilized their product, understood their market, and now appear to be in a healthy scaling phase.

The Summary: Product Leadership Is Core Company Strategy

Product leadership in deep tech is not a function. It's not a title. It's a strategic stance.

It means: respecting the complexity of what you're building, sequencing your commercialization correctly, investing into true product adoption, resisting the pressure to sell before you have something worth selling, and building the organizational discipline to learn before you earn.

The companies that will define the next generation of robotics and deep tech — in Europe and globally — will not be the ones that sold like hell (which often translates to overselling the vision). They'll be the ones that learned with rigor, built with discipline, and commercialized when they were ready. Ultimately, perhaps paradoxically, this rigor and discipline leads to faster and sustainable commercial success.

The hard part is that "ready" doesn't announce itself. You have to decide to define it, hold to it, and resist the many forces that push you past it before you've earned the right.

Robert MacKenzie is an executive leader (CPO/CTO) with deep experience scaling engineering organizations in robotics and AI, including 4.5 years as CPO/CTO Solutions at ANYbotics. He is a partner at ellipsis Venture, a robotics-focused investment firm based in Zurich, Switzerland.

Originally published in the Technology Company Leadership newsletter on LinkedIn on 14 April 2026. Read it on LinkedIn.

item.title: Healthily Challenging: The Leadership Setup Where People Truly Thrive
item.description: Leadership is too often framed as a choice between pushing hard for results or protecting well-being. One path risks burnout, the other stagnation. In my experience, the binary is wrong and lazy leadership. I suggest aiming for a third way. It’s one that I call creating a healthi
item.content:encoded:
Leadership is too often framed as a choice between pushing hard for results or protecting well-being. One path risks burnout, the other stagnation. In my experience, the binary is wrong and lazy leadership. I suggest aiming for a third way. It’s one that I call creating a healthily challenging environment, in which excellence and ambition must exist, yet are balanced with health and headspace.

Walk into any fast-scaling company and you can feel it almost immediately. There is a hum of ambition, the energy of bright people chasing big goals, and, sometimes, the undertow of stress that threatens to pull it all apart. Early reports about teams adopting AI-enabled tools and workflows suggest that this hum is even intensifying as the same people or fewer are trying to achieve and deliver more, faster.

Understanding a Healthily Challenging System

I chose the term “healthily challenging" consciously to help self-correct from toxic extremes. When the challenges become the wrong kind or too many, it isn’t healthy and requires correction. When “healthy” begins to drift into “comfortable”, the beneficial amount of ambition and challenges is lost and requires correction.

The simplest metaphor for “Healthy Stress vs. Constant Stress” I’ve found is The Balloon Test:

  • With zero air, the balloon is limp and lifeless, and represents a team without energy or challenge.
  • With constant, excessive air, the balloon inevitably bursts and represents a team/culture of relentless pressure, sleepless nights, and silent disengagement.
  • With the right amount of air, the balloon is full, resilient, and ready to bounce back.

A healthily challenging environment is that third balloon. There’s tension, but the right kind that’s balanced with purpose, which is what fuels curiosity, collaboration, and growth.

Healthily challenging is a place where ambition is tangible but not toxic, where people feel stretched but not broken, and where excellence and humanity reinforce each other rather than compete. Going deeper, it’s a place where even the terms ambition or challenge are consciously defined and can (and should) change form from phase to phase.

  • The challenge of developing through unknowns e.g. explorative development of a new technology, algorithm or some valuable breakthrough
  • The challenge of meeting a key deadline or outcome on time e.g. project delivery or sales target
  • The challenge of change and learning e.g. shifting behavior, learning and execution to effectively adopt AI
  • The challenge of delivering with excellence and accepting reasonable delay e.g. prioritizing quality over time when delivering a product

Being clear on the current challenge is often key to success. For example, the challenge of finishing an R&D development project on cue, but requiring the project to achieve explorative breakthroughs are often incompatible challenges.

Guided Autonomy: The Leadership Style Behind “Healthily Challenging”

At the core of this approach is something I call guided autonomy.

Too often, leadership is confused with control. It can be assumed that if leaders don’t prescribe the “how,” things will fall apart. Yet, a leader who makes all the decisions is a bottleneck, not a leader. Then there is the opposite. Yet a leader who sets no direction and calls it "empowerment" is abdicating, not leading. So, leaders should determine the “what” not that "how", right? No, that’s oversimplified. I believe that great leaders are accountable for the “what” (i.e. goals, results) and know how to build and guide a system to find and define the right goals with the right mix of direction (i.e. coming from leader) and collaboration (i.e. coming from others). When well orchestrated, I am convinced that this leads to better goals, with stronger collective understanding and buy-in.

So, for me, guided autonomy starts with setting clear goals together. Creating the right top-down, bottom-up, collective vs. independent planning system is a book for itself. However, one cheat code I have found is to hire and train people to work toward and think in goals and outcomes, not just tasks. I look for people who can self-coordinate, adapt, and innovate their way toward results, which is often a great first step toward developing the ability to coordinate others.

Then, the leader’s job can shift. Instead of being the bottleneck (setting all goals, making all decisions), the leader becomes the orchestrator: shaping direction, removing clutter, and building a culture where curiosity and constructive challenge are encouraged.

This is one contributing factor that creates what psychologists call psychological safety. Importantly, it’s not comfort. It’s the ability to constructively challenge and disagree without fear of retribution. In well-resourced setups, it expands to the safety to stretch, experiment, and even fail in pursuit of excellence and results, with the “pursuit of excellence and results” a key aspect (see the section above about consciously defining challenges). Other contributing factors to psychological safety include (but are not limited to), acting upon feedback to change a system, then delivering; responding constructively when team members challenge ideas; providing feedback and setting clear boundaries when team members disagree in destructive instead of constructive ways.

When Culture Shows Up

Culture is often misunderstood. Too many organizations equate it with social events, office design, or a handful of “values on the wall.” In my book, culture is simply the way we work and interact, especially when things aren’t going well.

That’s when stories are formed! How people step up under pressure, how leaders respond to mistakes, how colleagues treat each other when deadlines loom, how we celebrate individual and collective victories, etc. I’ve seen both sides.

In one instance, I built a project team and coached the Project Lead on guided autonomy. The team was delivering a company-saving set of deliverables to Google. It was a complex project and as with every project had to navigate unexpected setbacks. Instead of finger-pointing or waiting for instructions, team members leaned into each other’s expertise, coordinated without dependence on central direction from the Project Lead, and continually turned near-crisis into a breakthrough. The culture had become self-reinforcing, especially since there was collective buy-in for the goals they set together, with leadership.

By contrast, I’ve also seen situations where ambition tipped into toxicity. Ownership became a burden rather than a privilege, and values turned rigid instead of guiding.

Culture, in such moments, is visceral and no longer theoretical. And the difference between healthy and toxic environments is rarely the size of the goal. It’s how the leader sets up the system around that goal.

The Tap on the Shoulder

One image that comes to mind is what it feels like when you’re deep in focused work, and someone taps you on the shoulder. If it happens rarely, it’s fine and even welcome. But if it happens constantly, it’s impossible to make progress. In over-challenging systems, when ambition is toxic, responding to someone tapping you on the shoulder can mean immediately falling behind on your work. Collaboration breaks down. Culture begins to suffer instead of support.

That’s what too much ambition, too many goals, or excessive complexity does to a team and much of this was covered in a previous article: The Hidden Magic of Unplanned Capacity. The key insight is to see healthily challenging environments as unclogged. They leave room for people to breathe, focus, and achieve something meaningful.

Leaders who master this balance aren’t lowering standards. On the contrary, they often achieve more excellence than their high-pressure peers. Why? Because people in healthily challenging environments aren’t merely surviving. They’re thriving, innovating, and collaborating with energy left in reserve.

In addition to “The Tap on the Shoulder”, here are a few other signals I've found reliable:

Healthy signals: People openly flag problems before they escalate. Learning is emphasized and failure is analyzed, not hidden. Decisions (and budgets) are distributed to those closest to the data and the learning loop. Disagreements happen, but end constructively and with actions. Disagreements in meetings don't end careers. People are stretched but not constantly exhausted. High performers stay and they recruit other high performers because they tell their networks it's a good place to do great work.

Unhealthy signals (often invisible from the outside): Meetings are harmonious, people stop asking questions, and decisions are thin. The same problems recur as teams avoid surfacing bad news. Output becomes toxic i.e. everything is about results, never about learning or true excellence/quality. There is a sense that leadership, while remaining truthful, is investing disproportionate energy into narratives and storytelling to make things seem that they fit. Turnover among the best people is higher than among the average. People say yes to everything (because disagreement is risky) and then quietly fail to deliver. Or they deliver, exhausted, and leave. Or they are exhausted and stay, but lack energy for the next batch of results.

So in closing, that's the setup I strive to create! A system where guided autonomy, psychological safety, and healthy challenge come together to deliver results and humanity.

After 30+ years of leading others, I profit from coming back to this one question worth asking honestly: Are you creating a balloon that can bounce or one about to burst?

Originally published in the Technology Company Leadership newsletter on LinkedIn on 17 March 2026. Read it on LinkedIn.

item.title: Should Switzerland embrace being the "CERN of robotics"?
item.description: Should Switzerland embrace being the "CERN of robotics" and become a landscape of indispensability in robotics?
item.content:encoded:
Should Switzerland embrace being the "CERN of robotics" and become a landscape of indispensability in robotics?

I've been thinking about this a lot lately while on the road with ellipsis.

The Swiss Startup Association's Startup-Agenda Schweiz says: "Startups in Switzerland seldom fail due to their ideas, but rather structural hurdles." The country optimises for creating companies, not scaling them. 31 of 42 startup exits in 2025 went to international buyers. Project Switzerland (a national initiative by Deep Tech Nation Switzerland) connecting scale-ups with unicorn founders, correctly identifies that true scaling expertise is still rare in Switzerland's startup ecosystem and difficult to access, especially in robotics. (PS - I am right here ladies and gents 🙂)

Some uncomfortable questions:

  • Are we trying to be something we are not?
  • Yes, we should improve at scaling, but are we strategically scaling in the right things?

Look at two of Europe's most valuable tech companies:

  • ARM never made a phone. It designed the architecture inside every phone.
  • ASML doesn't make chips. It makes the only machines that can make advanced chips.

Neither out-scaled the US or Asia. Both became indispensable by owning a layer nobody else could replicate.

Should we be doing this more consciously in Switzerland?

  • Sevensense → visual navigation in ABB's/Softbank’s global robotics platform. Team stayed in Zurich.
  • Embotech → autonomous vehicle control in multiple BMW factories.
  • Flexion Robotics → humanoid robot control systems. Not building robots. Building the cognition inside them.
  • mimic → dexterous hands that learn to work by watching. The manipulation layer every robot will need.

The Swiss watchmaking model applied to robotics: you don't need to make the most watches. You need to make the ones others can't replicate.

I think:

  • Companies that will thrive here are those with narrow verticals, deep technical moats, and Swiss credibility in safety-critical, regulated markets.
  • Companies building full robotics solutions in Switzerland, then opening an office in the US to scale is not a doomed play, but it’s a hard one and maybe doesn’t play to our ecosystem’s real strengths.

So, is this a signal to play a different game?

What do you think: does Switzerland need its own robotics unicorn, or is creating a "landscape of indispensability" a stronger way forward?

Originally posted on LinkedIn on 11 March 2026. Read it on LinkedIn.

item.title: The Hidden Magic of Unplanned Capacity: Push teams to their potential, not their limits
item.description: Imagine walking into a top CEO’s office decades ago. You might see an executive assistant sitting calmly, apparently with little to do. Then suddenly the phone rings or an urgent request comes in and they leap into action, handling the issue in minutes. The CEO’s day keeps hummin
item.content:encoded:
Imagine walking into a top CEO’s office decades ago. You might see an executive assistant sitting calmly, apparently with little to do. Then suddenly the phone rings or an urgent request comes in and they leap into action, handling the issue in minutes. The CEO’s day keeps humming along smoothly. That idle-looking time wasn’t wasted at all; it was slack, extra capacity that allowed instant responsiveness and full followthrough. If that assistant had been 100% busy with other tasks, the CEO’s critical request would have had to wait, slowing down important decisions. Today, many workplaces seem to have lost this wiggle room, pushing every team and individual to full capacity.

It’s time to rediscover the hidden magic of unplanned capacity and why not pushing your team to the brink will positively transform performance.

The 100% Utilization Myth

The real goal is 100% output. However, in our efficiency-obsessed work culture, an all-too-common belief is that maximizing everyone’s workload maximizes output. Fill every hour with assigned tasks, eliminate any idle time, and you’ve achieved peak productivity, right? Wrong. Scheduling your team at 100% capacity is a great way to ensure that nothing will be delivered on time.

One reason 100% utilization backfires is simple queueing theory. Systems (or teams) with no slack become disastrously unresponsive when anything new arises. Why? Because as a system nears full utilization, wait times for new tasks skyrocket exponentially.

External Example: Think of a hospital emergency room: at 50% usage, a new patient is seen quickly; at 90%+ usage, incoming patients wait much longer. At 100% capacity, even an expected sneeze can halt progress.

Personal Example: When deploying autonomous robots in industrial facilities, I learned this lesson viscerally. A robotics engineer (or project team) at 100% capacity meant to work on a new robotic capability, could often handle some debugging of a surprise in-field issue, but was often over-capacity if manufacturing additionally needed updates to their testing software. By the time they context-switched, the production line was impacted. Teams with buffer could swarm problems immediately, which was the difference between minutes of downtime and hours.

The Ownership Paradox

Here's where the 100% utilization trap becomes insidious. It creates impossible no-win situations.

Consider the robotics engineer from above. If they prioritized their main goal (the new robotic capability), the Head of Production criticized their lack of ownership and support. If they prioritized production issues, their project lead questioned their ownership to the main goal when deliverables slipped.

The paradox: In both cases, the engineer showed full ownership. But operating at full capacity created the perception of no ownership; a lose-lose for the organization and the individual, yet almost entirely the fault of the organizational dynamic.

The human summary: People obviously aren’t machines. An industrial robot might sustain 100% utilization, but humans degrade under such strain. Overworked teams become less productive. Fatigue, context-switching, no room to do your best, the inability to help/be helped, etc. all lead to stress, mistakes, rework. All goals remain underachieved in some way.

Why Slack Time = Peak Performance

As counterintuitive as it sounds, the highest-performing teams leave slack in their schedule. This consciously “unplanned capacity” is the secret sauce behind greater innovation, agility, and resilience. When people have some breathing room, amazing things happen:

  1. Breakthrough Innovation. With effective guidance, team members explore better ways to reach outcomes. Even when starting with known methods (instead of experimental methods), the freedom to circle back and find improvements benefits everyone. And when predictable methods fail, having space to explore alternatives becomes essential.
  2. Agility and Problem-Solving. Slack is critical for survival in a dynamic environment. As our businesses today face constant changes, sudden customer escalations, production bugs, new opportunities that demand quick turnaround. If your team has zero free capacity, you can’t respond in time. By the time you drop something to address the new fire, you’ve already missed the window or disrupted other commitments (see the previous paradox). On the other hand, a team with a bit of slack can absorb shocks. Slack time is what turns “we can’t squeeze this in” into “we’re on this, no problem.”
  3. Quality, Continuous Learning and Improvement. Ever notice how less rush means better work? Teams experience this too. Unscheduled time enables improving AI agents, refactoring messy code, updating documentation, and fixing small issues before they grow—proactive maintenance that gets skipped when everyone is overloaded. The result: higher quality output and less technical debt. They "slowed down to speed up". This is only possible with spare capacity or by planning it into the 80% limit. Routine training and learning require time. If every moment is booked, employees never learn new tools or adopt better practices. Slack time lets teams invest in themselves, improving processes and skills that compound over time.
  4. Employee Well-Being, Collaboration, and Engagement. Perhaps most importantly, humane pacing drives motivation and creativity. When people aren't relentlessly grinding, they have time to think deeply and anticipate problems.

Embracing Slack: How Leaders Can Unleash Hidden Capacity

Shifting from a 100%-booked culture to one that embraces unplanned capacity requires a mindset change at the top. Company leaders must redefine what productivity looks like, dispelling the notion that “idle time” is wasted time.

Leaders should focus on results achieved, not hours worked or tasks in motion. Here are a few ways to put this into practice:

Model It: Set the Example. If you’re a leader/manager, resist the urge to fill your own calendar to the brim. When your team sees that you value reflection and sane work hours, they’ll feel permission to do the same. This starts with the CEO. A CEO working beyond healthy capacity often injects work at the wrong moment, unknowingly becoming a disruptor rather than an enabler.

Define It: Visualize goals and distinguish them from toil. Then toil can be planned into the 80%. Otherwise, it's layered on top and the slack disappears before it exists.

Communicate It: Talk About the Why. Explain to your team why you are intentionally leaving a buffer in plans. Share the data that running at 70-80% capacity (instead of 100%) is proven to reduce errors and burnout while maintaining throughput. When people understand that slack is a strategic choice, not an accident of under-planning, they’ll support it.

Protect It: Guard the Slack. It’s very easy for slack time to get stolen by new “urgent” asks or scope creep. Be vigilant. If you’ve committed to, say, Fridays being meeting-free or 10% of each sprint unassigned, stick to it. Encourage team members to use slack time for forward-looking work: learning, improving systems, or tackling that “important but not urgent” project that often gets neglected.

Recognize It: Reward Outcomes, Not Busyness. Adjust what behaviours get praise and reward in your organization. Instead of applauding the hero who stays until midnight (a sign of an overloaded system), praise the planner who delivered a quality project without drama. Make it clear that continuous crunch mode is not a badge of honour. Celebrate clever solutions, innovations, and improvements, many of which arise from slack.

Formalize It: Use Slack for Development. Consider formalizing some slack in the form of innovation time or improvement sprints. Hackathons, 20% time, “refactoring Fridays,” or regular R&D days signal that it’s okay to work on non-project tasks. Just be sure to give guidance so that time is used meaningfully, as not everyone immediately knows how to manage open-ended freedom.

Balance matters. Too much slack can lead to waste if not channeled well. But most organizations risk the opposite: not enough slack. The evidence is overwhelming that moderate slack (10-20% of work hours) yields outsized benefits in innovation, quality, and team health. The 80% utilization mark often emerges as the upper limit before wait times and stress rise exponentially. Pushing your team slightly less helps them accomplish more long-term.

Conclusion: Less Is More, for Sustainable Success

In an era where "busy" is a status symbol, championing slack time feels like heresy. But unplanned capacity is becoming a recognized advantage of high-performing teams. We achieve more in the long run with slack; we're "more productive when we don't try to be productive all the time." Not pushing people to their limits gives them space to excel, to think, experiment, recover, and rise to each challenge fully ready. Businesses that internalize this and treat their employees not as factory machines but as creative, thinking humans are seeing the payoff in agility and innovation.

So next time you’re planning a project or a quarter, leave a little unplanned capacity on purpose. Don’t cram the jar full of rocks; leave some spaces. Your team’s energy and ingenuity will fill them in ways you couldn’t have predicted and the results. In the end, keeping your team a little under capacity is not a wasted opportunity. It’s what primes them to seize the best opportunities when they arise. That is the paradoxical winning formula: by focusing on the right outcomes, your team can achieve so much more.

Push teams to their potential, not their limits.

Not sure where your organization stands? Try this Quick Check.

A Quick Check: Does Your Team Have Slack?

  • Can your team absorb an urgent request this week without dropping commitments?
  • When was the last time someone had time to improve a process (not just execute it)?
  • Do people routinely work after hours to "catch up"? Or worse, have they given up trying?

Sources

  • Reclaiming Organizational Capacity
  • Efficiency is the Enemy
  • Engineering Productivity Paradox
  • Queuing Theory, Slack and Utilisation
  • Wiki: Queuing Theory / Utilization Effect In queuing theory there’s a well-known principle: as system utilization approaches 100%, throughput plummets and cycle times skyrocket. Even going above ~80-85% utilization creates nonlinear delays. This is why factories, call centers, and teams keep “slack capacity.” This is often illustrated by Kingman’s Formula or the Utilization Law in queueing theory.
  • Theory of Constraints (TOC) TOC says the system’s throughput is determined by its most constrained resource. If every resource is scheduled to 100%, any variability will create bottlenecks. Allowing slack (protecting capacity at the constraint) keeps flow moving.
  • Little’s Law (Lean / Kanban) In lean/agile circles, Little’s Law (Work in Progress, WIP = Throughput × Cycle Time) is often used to explain why too much WIP slows the system. By limiting WIP to ~70% of team capacity, flow is faster and smoother.

item.title: High-Velocity Decision-Making for Individuals and Teams
item.description: Most teams don’t suffer from a lack of decisions. They suffer from decisions that are too slow, leaving less time for real execution. The good news is that you don’t need your whole organization to change before you speed things up.
item.content:encoded:
Most teams don’t suffer from a lack of decisions. They suffer from decisions that are too slow, leaving less time for real execution. The good news is that you don’t need your whole organization to change before you speed things up.

Based on repeated personal success, this article explores how Amazon’s “high-velocity decision-making” can be applied to individuals and teams. A future article will explore how high-velocity decision making can be established as an organization.

Why aim for high-velocity decisions at the team level?

Some may fear chaos and decisions “being made everywhere.” Let’s be honest! Your organization’s decision-making is probably already chaotic and decisions are already being made everywhere, even though you may have structures, documentation, etc. in place. So, even if you cannot change your organization, you can change your team environment and behavior! Consider:

  • Isn’t it unavoidable that decisions are being made everywhere? Every line of code from a developer (or accepting code from an AI co-pilot) is a type of decision. Every purchase for this instead of that is a type of decision. Every meeting method or invitation if a meeting should be held is a decision (or an indecision).
  • If decisions are already being made everywhere, the real question is: Will they be made consciously and effectively, or slowly and chaotically?

Applying high-velocity decision-making is a way of shifting and potentially simplifying your decision-making framework in such a way that embraces “decisions being made everywhere” as a desirable and unavoidable fact. By “simply” becoming conscious about the type of decisions to make, you open yourself up to the possibility of supercharging your own decision-making and that of your organization (if fully embraced by the organization).

Some of the benefits for favouring high-velocity decision-making in your team:

  • You as a team lead are less-burdened by decisions that honestly don’t require you
  • Higher engagement and fulfillment of individuals and teams, now empowered to reach decisions via a simple guideline
  • Generally, a vast reduction in process for the majority of decisions that don’t require this (see Two-Way decisions)
  • Specifically, an increase in quality decision tracking and outcome for those few decisions that profit from careful decision-making (see One-Way decisions)
  • An increase in the quality of decision-making increases via continual practice and empowerment

Let’s start with the underlying problem: Slow Decision-Making.

Slow Decision-Making:

One extreme of slow decision-making is indecision. A variety of factors can cause slow decision-making, which include

  • Fear of consequences e.g. based on uncertainty of outcomes
  • Over-analysis / perfectionism e.g. too much discussion as a form of looking for data or consensus with many opinions
  • Lack of decision-making boundaries e.g. a belief that Team Leads must decide everything

One obvious and visible symptom of this is a constant back and forth, which can mean i) no clear process or responsibility or ii) the process is too complex and/or subjective.

Concepts for Achieving High-Velocity Decision-Making

ONE: Is the topic/decision a one-way or two-way decision?

A “local” scope could often point to two-way decisions, while “global” scopes will tend to be one-way decisions. Here is more helpful information side-by-side.

Comparison of one-way and two-way decision types.

Link: Integrative Decision Making

TWO: Decisions are not selections (70–90 rule)

Decide, don’t select! If you wait for 90+% of the data, you’re selecting, not deciding. At ~70%, pull the trigger. Leadership means accepting residual risk.

Here are some implementation tips:

  • 70% data is a mental model. Aim for less if you’re ready to risk the decision earlier e.g. taking a bet
  • Default to “testing” the outcome of your decision over “cognitively blocking” the decision and preventing it from being tested
  • Embrace that it is hard to predict the new. It is much easier to predict what won't change (people want to feel safe, customers want low prices, etc.). This can help cut through some complexity

THREE: Decisions must be reached!

You don’t always have to be the decider. At the team level, engagement increases when team members are empowered to ensure that decisions are reached. Actively train and reward a team-wide mentality that those involved actively contribute to a decision being reached. Favourable decisions are rarely reached by passively waiting for others to decide. Thinking that a team lead/manager knows it all and should decide all is outdated and ignores modern complexity. Oversimplified, a decision can be reached by:

  • One extreme = make all decisions as a leader (i.e. centralized power, which I don’t recommend)
  • A better path = establish simple mechanisms and steps to make sure a group and individuals can reach decisions
  • The golden mix = master the simple mechanisms and identifying decision types, enable self-decision and expert group facilitation toward the best decision outcomes

FOUR: Involve only decision contributors, no observers

Don’t mix the two. Even when looking for the right group of contributors, don’t feel compelled to invite all of them. Knowing how to invite the contributors and politely excluding observers can be surprisingly hard. Having a reputation of providing clear information to stakeholders can buffer this, as non-invited people will rely on your communication post-decision. Here are some implementation tips:

  • Risk not involving (e.g. think about only needing 70% of the right data)
  • Look for a majority of contributors to make a decision and share the consequences
  • Maybe you, alone, represent that “majority”
  • When in doubt, look for the “metric owner” to decide, probably a person with excellent access to the right data for informing a decision
  • Non-involved contributors (e.g. busy, sick) and observers can and should be selectively informed outside of the main decision-making moment, via a video or AI-generated meeting summaries. Using meetings to inform “everyone” is a killer of meeting purpose and efficiency

Some extra guidance in a nutshell:

  • Involve contributors (data, responsibility, consequences)
  • Exclude observers (curious, interested, not accountable)

FIVE: Seek a lack of valid objection instead of a universal agreement

Again, deciding is about taking risks. The first risk is sharing a proposal, such that you risk having the wrong proposal. Your goal must be the right proposal, either through directly making a great proposal and/or via integrating feedback. A solid, well-integrated proposal will almost always overcome or eliminate objections.

However, don’t fear objections as they are also a form of feedback and should only block the final decision of accepting a proposal if the objection is valid.

Valid objections must have a clear rule set, often centred around the logic that acceptance of the proposal would not allow learning from testing and/or immediately cause measurable harm to an organizational entity (e.g. a person, a team or the organization as a whole).

  • Make a solid proposal and communicate it clearly with decision contributors
  • Again, we are reminded of the power of frameworks like Integrative Decision-Making (IDM), which promote reaching decisions and rapidly testing things in action. If the decision/change doesn’t seem to work, inject a better proposal into the IDM process. With IDM, only valid objections can stop your proposal

In the AWS framework, a variation on this theme for avoiding consensus is known as disagree and commit. Either the person pushing to reach a decision asks for such a commitment or the person in disagreement realizes that it's healthier to move forward, help the decision succeed and learn quickly from the decision outcomes, instead of continue to disagree upfront.

In summary, behaving like a high-velocity, high-quality decision maker could be as easy as following this recipe:

  • Understand if One or Two-Way - emphasize velocity for two-way decisions.
  • Decide! Don’t Select - lead toward a decision and embrace smart risk.
  • Find the Best Truth & Contributors - who is closest to the right information?
  • Challenge Group Thinking - resist the overrated importance of harmony.
  • Have Courage - be great at dealing with healthy conflict.
  • Minimize Regrets - test, learn, move on, improve, then make the next better decision.

Decide, don’t select! If you wait for 90+% of the data, you’re selecting, not deciding. At ~70%, pull the trigger. Leadership means accepting residual risk.

Ready to reach some decisions? Then take action! Pick one upcoming decision in your team. Classify it as one-way or two-way. Apply velocity if it’s two-way. Notice the difference. Once you start practicing this, you’ll see how quickly your team gains speed, confidence, and clarity. High-velocity decision-making doesn’t just move work forward, it builds trust, ownership, and resilience.

Sources and Additional Resources

  • Lessons from Amazon on High-Velocity and High-Quality Decision-Making
  • https://productlessons.medium.com/lessons-from-amazon-on-high-velocity-and-high-quality-decision-making-f1d5715908d1
  • https://rufuspollock.com/2020/05/18/jeff-bezos-fast-high-quality-decision-making/

This is article #2 in a three-part series on decision-making.

  1. Integrative Decision-Making (Bits of Holacracy for Any Organization)
  2. High-Velocity Decision-Making for Individuals and Teams
  3. Orchestrating Decision-Making in Your Organization

item.title: Integrative Decision-Making (Bits of Holacracy for Any Organization)
item.description: In my years of leadership across various organizations, I've encountered numerous decision-making frameworks. Among them, Integrative Decision-Making (IDM) from Holacracy stands out for its structured approach to processing proposals and addressing tensions within teams. During m
item.content:encoded:
In my years of leadership across various organizations, I've encountered numerous decision-making frameworks. Among them, Integrative Decision-Making (IDM) from Holacracy stands out for its structured approach to processing proposals and addressing tensions within teams. During my time at Labster we scaled the entire organization globally using Holacracy as our main underlying system for running our organization and IDM was an integral part. ANYbotics was generally less open to the distributed responsibility and principles of Holacracy. Nonetheless, I adapted bits of Holacracy for ANYbotics, like Integrative Decision-Making and Tactical Meetings (see previous newsletter article), which were quickly and effectively adopted within my division.

So, even if your organization hasn't adopted or isn't open to the concepts of Holacracy, IDM offers valuable insights and practices that can enhance your decision-making processes, especially for one-way decisions and structural/governance changes in teams.

Understanding Integrative Decision-Making

At its core, IDM is designed to efficiently resolve tensions, defined as perceived gaps between the current state and a desired state, by following a clear, step-by-step process. Instead of blocking change with massively entangled topics, this step-by-step process involves processing one tension at a time, in an attempt to unravel complexity and support dynamic change. Furthermore, IDM ensures that all voices are heard without descending into unproductive debates or consensus-seeking paralysis. While IDM is overkill for daily, straightforward decisions (see Two-Way Decisions in future articles), it is ideal for consequential decisions requiring careful consideration, involvement and input from a group.

The IDM Process: A Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Present Proposal: The proposer articulates a specific proposal to address a tension they've identified. It's crucial that this proposal is concrete and actionable.
  2. Clarifying Questions: Participants ask questions to understand the proposal better. This is only for clarifying inquiries and not the stage for opinions or reactions.
  3. Reaction Round: One-by-one, each participant provides their initial reactions to the proposal. These are individual perspectives, ideally based on their role in the process, shared without discussion or interruption. Participants can pass and/or keep their reactions very short.
  4. Amend and Clarify: The proposer has an opportunity to modify the proposal based on the feedback received, ensuring it more closely considers the group's needs and concerns, ideally strengthening the proposal's ability to resolve the related tension. While the proposer must consider amendment, the proposer is not forced to amend or compromise.
  5. Objection Round: Participants can raise objections if they foresee and can prove potential harm or unintended consequences resulting from the proposal. What counts as a valid objection or proof of harm is carefully regulated via the process (Hint: Personal objections don't count).
  6. Integration: If valid objections arise, the team collaborates to adjust the proposal, integrating input to find a solution that works for everyone. If the integration is complex and for meeting efficiency, the facilitator can end this meeting by asking the proposer to first work on an improved proposal to process in a future meeting.

Here is the full online process from HolacracyOne.

What makes IDM particularly powerful is how it reshapes the dynamics of group interaction. Participants are asked to listen and clarify first, before reacting, slowing the reflex to defend or dismiss. When reactions are shared, the proposer listens without rebuttal and later reflects aloud on what they heard. This encourages humility and shared ownership over the proposal's evolution.

The objection round introduces another hidden gem: a logical framework for determining whether an objection is valid. Personal discomfort isn't enough! Objections must point to potential harm and pass structured tests. When this is facilitated well, it can create aha! moments. Dominant voices discover their opinions aren’t vetoes, and quieter participants realize their thoughtful concerns can help reach meaningful decisions. In this way, IDM not only produces better decisions, it cultivates a culture of trust, respect, and progress.

I have seen groups transform from stuck and embattled to aligned on common goals and enlightened in under 30 minutes, simply because IDM gave every voice structure and space.

Benefits of Integrative Decision-Making

  • Efficiency: By following a structured process, decisions are reached more swiftly, reducing the time spent in meetings.
  • Clarity: Each step has a defined purpose, ensuring that discussions remain focused and productive.
  • Inclusivity: All contributors to reaching a decision have a voice, fostering a sense of ownership and commitment to the decisions made. No one voice, ego, or powerful job title dominates.
  • Adaptability: The process allows for continuous evolution, accommodating new information and changing circumstances. The same process can be used to reverse a change after a period of testing.
  • Learning: Perhaps one of IDM’s most underrated benefits is how it reshapes team dynamics over time. Because the process encourages structured listening, logical reflection, and shared accountability, participants begin to think differently, comparing IDM to more chaotic or unstructured processes that they experience. Over time, individuals (and groups) learn to separate role-based reasoning from personal ego, and teams collectively improve how they process complexity and make decisions.

Key Considerations for Effective Execution

While IDM offers a robust framework, its success hinges on mindful implementation:

  • Facilitation: A skilled facilitator is essential to guide the process, ensuring adherence to each step and maintaining a respectful environment. Participants often require strong guidance on when to listen vs. when to share their input. Especially the objection round requires strong facilitation when/if strong egos wish to block proposals based on non-valid objections.
  • Training: Team members should be educated on the IDM process to participate effectively and understand their roles within it.
  • Cultural Alignment: Assess whether IDM aligns with your organization's culture and values. While adaptable, its principles should resonate with your team's dynamics.
  • Commitment to the Process: Consistency is key. Regular application of IDM fosters familiarity and trust in the process, leading to better outcomes over time.

Key Differences of IDM in Holacratic vs Other Organizations

The IDM method can be used in any organization. However, its application will feel enhanced in a Holacracy-powered environment. Here are three key distinctions I’ve observed:

Roles vs. Titles (or Egos)

In Holacracy, people are trained to think and act through their roles, not only their job titles or personal identities. This means that when participating in IDM, you speak and decide as the role you're inhabiting, not as your whole self or your highest-ranking title. For instance, I might carry both a “Team Lead” and an “Engineer” role. As a Team Lead, I might instinctively want to retain control. But as an Engineer, I may see that a proposal clearly improves outcomes for everyone, even if it transforms leadership control. IDM provides a structured way to bring those role-based perspectives forward, making space for better decisions and less ego-driven friction.

Tooling and Shared Context

You don’t need special tools to decide via IDM. However, holacratic organizations typically use specialized software (like GlassFrog or HolaSpirit) to document every role’s scope, purpose, and accountabilities. This tooling is a living, trusted source of truth that additionally informs all governance and enhances decision-making. In contrast, traditional organizations often lack a similar system. When only IDM is introduced in organizations without a referable shared context (e.g. clear role definitions, transparent governance) enacting the decision outcome may not be as immediate and straightforward.

Pace and Embedding of Change

Holacracy is designed for continuous evolution and is biased to accept a proposal unless it can be proven that testing a proposal causes immediate harm to the organization. So, once a decision is made through IDM, it’s typically documented immediately and becomes part of the operational fabric; visible and actionable for everyone. Outside of Holacracy, even great decisions often face delays: waiting for buy-in, documentation, or communication. Without integrated tooling or process discipline, change can lose momentum or stay siloed.

Final Thoughts

Integrative Decision-Making offers a pathway to more democratic, efficient, and effective decision-making within teams. By embracing its structured approach, groups can navigate complexities with greater agility and cohesion. Whether or not Holacracy is part of your organizational framework, IDM's principles can be a valuable addition to your decision-making toolkit.

Personally, I love IDM and I have many more insights to share that don't fit into this one article. You're invited to engage with me if you wish to learn more (or help me learn more).

Sources and Additional Resources

  • Holacracy's Radically Different Decision-Making Process (Video)
  • https://www.holacracy.org/r/governance-meeting-process
  • https://www.talkspirit.com/blog/integrative-decision-making-vs-consensus
  • https://www.walkme.com/blog/holacratic-organizational-structure

  2. High-Velocity Decision-Making for Individuals and Teams
