item.title: Higher Engagement with Tactical Meetings (Bits of Holacracy for Any Organization)
item.description: Tired of team meetings that drag on, achieve little, and leave people disengaged? What if you could transform them into short, energizing sessions where every voice is heard and where real progress is made?
item.content:encoded:
Tired of team meetings that drag on, achieve little, and leave people disengaged? What if you could transform them into short, energizing sessions where every voice is heard and where real progress is made?

Enter the Tactical Meeting. Originating from Holacracy, this meeting format works surprisingly well even in traditional hierarchies when wisely tweaked.

In this article, I’ll share how I’ve used and adapted Tactical Meetings, as well as why I believe it’s one of the most powerful formats for operational alignment, ,mostly independent of the underlying organizational system. This article is not meant as a critique or comparison of other valid meeting formats used in technology companies and other organizations e.g., Scrum ceremonies, steering committees. I don't explore or explain Holacracy.

Will you be able to run a Tactical Meeting as described here after reading this article? Maybe. My true intention is to create a few “Aha!” moments share my experience on how to bring this type of meeting to life, effectively. I hope to inspire you to experiment with this meeting format in your organization or team.

My Encounter with Tactical Meetings

While completing my graduate studies and early in my career, I received formal training in facilitation, moderation, and didactics (the science of teaching and knowledge transfer). I then spent years professionally designing and leading international leadership seminars, strategic planning workshops, and train-the-trainer programs. Through this, I built a strong foundation in group facilitation and effective meeting design. As I moved into formal leadership roles, I leaned on these skills, adapting and evolving them to lead teams, cross-functional groups, and entire organizations effectively.

Although I believe to have consistently operated at a fairly high level of meeting quality or facilitation quality, my first encounter with Tactical Meetings à la Holacracy in 2016 Labster was eye-opening. I was immediately drawn to the clarity and efficiency of this format, especially the way it centers around the principle of “listen to understand.” When I moved to ANYbotics, I successfully tweaked this methodology for use in a non-holacratic organization.

HolacracyOne does a fantastic job of describing the concept and process of Tactical Meetings in detail:

  • Tactical Meeting purpose and key features
  • Official process explanation
  • Reference card for facilitators

For readers unfamiliar with Tactical Meetings and wishing to rely on my article, here’s my summary and interpretation:

Tactical Meeting Purpose & Why They are Special

Tactical meetings exist to move the operational work of a team forward by regularly sensing current and upcoming issues, then triaging those issues efficiently.

Tactical Meetings are consciously designed and facilitated to allow team members to surface, share, and connect information in such a manner that targeted actions can be more easily defined without long diverging conversations or having someone dominate the space.

Tactical Meeting Structure and Flow

The basic structure of the meeting can be broken down into three main features:

Listening to Understand: The goal is for the participants to obtain a current overview of the team’s data (e.g. metrics, OKR progress), the major and minor issues, and even each other’s state of mind for the meeting. This phase is brief and yet everyone speaks! My teams aimed for a maximum of 20 minutes in total. Doing the math, in a meeting of ca. 6 people, each person had 2-3 minutes to provide a relevant overview for agenda consideration.

This phase should not be used for classical updates e.g. reporting on progress. Instead, people mention the achieved outcome(s) to celebrate, if help is needed, and/or if new delays are about to occur. This structure establishes a basis for collaboration i.e. how can I/we help?

The outcome should be a collective sense of the most important topics to address in the meeting.

Agenda Building: There should be a conscious moment to identify the first, maybe second most important collective issues to process. However, this phase of agenda building runs parallel for the rest of the meeting. As the targeted discussions unfold, clearer, separate issues may arise that impact the ordering of the agenda items.

Targeted Discussions and Actions: In this phase, the facilitator and group work together to stay on topic, working to achieve just enough discussion to understand the issue so that sensible actions can be defined. Generally, the issues in the tactical meeting arise because it wasn’t possible to solve them via ongoing, day-to-day collaboration. Therefore, they are often relevant to and/or require the majority of the group.

The outcome is a set of actions that are asynchronously worked on outside the tactical, unless immediate resolution is possible. It is not an outcome of the tactical meeting to spend the time solving the problem. Rather, the team works to obtain what they need to solve the problem outside the tactical, yet empowered via the tactical.

I have summarized my suggested flow and approach in the following 1-page overview, which can be used as a meeting guide and training tool for those looking to adopt.

My 1-page overview for Tactical Meetings

The Magic of Making Tactical Meetings Work

Like every tool and method, excellent execution of the method, not merely following the method instructions, leads to the desired results. Personally, I find the approach to Tactical Meetings quite straightforward. Nonetheless, over the years I have identified key elements that help increase meeting success and higher adoption of the Tactical Meeting style.

The Power of Clear Goals and Planning

Obviously, any type of team meeting will work better when the strategic goals, resulting from effective yearly and/or quarterly planning, are clear to the team. If your organization's or team’s strategic planning has not been effective, this Tactical Meeting format won’t fix that. However, applying the Tactical Meeting format may improve your team’s interaction, locally, within an otherwise chaotic system. The purpose of Tactical Meetings is to move operational work forward, ideally within a clear-enough strategic framework. If you sense that your team is trying to set strategic goals in the tactical meetings, your team won’t feel the full benefit of Tactical Meetings and the problem lies elsewhere e.g. in your approach to strategic planning.

Note: While exploring an issue it would be a perfectly valid Tactical Meeting outcome to create an action requiring a review of a strategic goal or the entire planning. However, that strategic review would happen e.g. in a workshop, not in the tactical.

In my organizations, we were effective at creating and adhering to yearly and quarterly OKRs. Over time, the combined clarity of our strategic goals and our Tactical Meeting effectiveness became so powerful that we required less than a 1-hour tactical every 2 weeks to achieve our goals and hit our metrics.

Distributed Responsibility

Rotating roles for the Tactical Meeting is powerful for increasing the understanding of the meeting method, as well as increasing meeting engagement. These roles additionally offer a chance to grow and train new skills for team members. Specifically, the Facilitator role should not default to the team’s lead. This aligns very well with my philosophy of consciously ensuring that team leads are never bottlenecks for their teams. This offers the additional benefit of the Team Lead being able to take on a different perspective. If your organization works with the principles of self-organization, Tactical Meetings are a great compliment. Yet, even if your organization doesn’t embrace self-organization, this Tactical Meeting method can still enhance your team meetings if the lead is willing to distribute responsibility within the meeting.

In my team(s), we rotated facilitators every quarter. If no one volunteered, we used an online tool to randomly select someone from a list of eligible candidates (i.e. those who hadn’t facilitated the previous quarter, weren’t away for most of the upcoming one). First-time facilitators received training and had to run a mock meeting with either me or the previous facilitator. The set of ceremonies became so beloved that no one volunteered on purpose; not to avoid the role, but because they genuinely enjoyed the suspense and ceremony of being randomly chosen.

Facilitation

Effective facilitation is probably the most important element. Especially because most other meetings and discussions flow differently than a Tactical Meeting, participants initially struggle with the concept of “first listening to understand”. On one hand, the Facilitator has to keep the special flow of a Tactical Meeting in mind. However, because everyone can refer to the same structured and documented flow, the Facilitator can afford to enforce certain behaviors in service of the meeting’s purpose.

For example, it is typical for participants to want to start discussions in the “Listening Round”. Here is where strong facilitation is essential to maintain the flow as intended. While the Facilitator is not alone in building the agenda, the Facilitator is accountable that an agenda is built and serves the purpose of the meeting. In the “Discussion and Action Round”, the Facilitator must achieve a tricky balance of allowing a discussion to flow, while helping to stop unnecessary discussion, without shutting down a useful discussion and without disengaging participants.

I found that these phrases are powerful for helping the Facilitator stay true to the purpose and flow of Tactical Meetings:

  • Check-In: What’s your state of mind and are you ready to go?
  • Listening: What are you celebrating or on which topics do you sense needing help?
  • Listening: Are you asking a clarifying question or starting a discussion?
  • Listening: We are still listening to understand. We may further discuss this topic later.
  • Listening: Please keep your overview brief. What is most relevant for a possible discussion?
  • Agenda: Based on comments and reactions, it seems [this issue] is most important. Let’s first spend [10 minutes] on that issue, then [5 minutes on issue 2] and see how far we have come.
  • Discussion and Actions: What do you need?
  • Discussion and Actions: This seems to be a two-person discussion or issue. Please record an action and solve this outside the tactical. Let’s move on.
  • Discussion and Actions: Do we understand the issue enough now to define actions?
  • Discussion and Actions: Do you have what you need?
  • Discussion and Actions: If feels like we’re solving something too complex for a tactical meeting. What is the right action and forum to work on this outside of this meeting?
  • Discussion and Actions: What have great actions, but who will do what by when?
  • General: Let’s given online participants a voice
  • Check-Out: What is your sense of today’s meeting? Where could we improve?
  • Check-Out: Was today’s meeting worthwhile? Why and how could we do better?

Psychological Safety

On one hand, Tactical Meetings work best in environments that encourage learning and don’t punish people for constructively speaking up. On the other hand, Tactical Meetings can be a great tool for establishing or strengthening psychological safety. The meeting elements of Check In and Check Out work best when team members can be themselves in a professional manner. It is oddly wonderful when team members honestly state in Check In “I am currently not concentrated, but ready enough to start”, and then hear something like “Wow, I enjoyed today’s meeting and it helped me focus my thoughts” in the Check-Out round. However, this is only possible when the team creates the time, space, and psychological safety.

Online Collaboration

To focus the collaboration and properly capture actions, it’s key to use a collaborative tool that follows the flow and structure of Tactical Meetings, ideally a digital tool as most teams today are hybrid. I have experience with two type of tools:

SaaS (GlassFrog): they provide agile software solutions for self-managed teams. One tool is tailored to the Holacracy Tactical Meeting, see image. The online SaaS nature of the tool is great for bringing everyone together centrally. However, the streamlined tool design, great for removing clutter, does allow links, but is not great at directly embedding rich information e.g. charts, videos, visuals.

A glimpse inside GlassFrog, an online tool for Tactical Meetings

Collaborative Document: GoogleDocs - it is easy (and essential) to recreate the Tactical Meeting flow in the GoogleDoc. This approach is great for embedding rich information (e.g. charts, videos, visuals), allows for centrally taking notes, as well as helping to highlight important issues (e.g. via comments, emojis). However, exactly this power can lead to the document becoming long and cluttered, causing participants to lose the flow.

From Ineffective and Boring to Effective and Energetic

If you and your team(s) can put the above into practice, I believe you’ll greatly increase your chances of sustainably moving away from common aspects that make meetings ineffective and not worthwhile. Here is an overview of the possible shifts FROM undesirable meeting aspects TO improvements resulting from good Tactical Meeting execution:

Limitations and Differences in My Approach

Even though I aim to stay true to the spirit of Holacracy’s Tactical Meetings, applying them in non-holacratic organizations naturally brings some adaptations and challenges.

Here are a few key limitations:

Egos and Power Dynamics: Like any change process, success depends heavily on the people involved, especially those in power. If a team lead resists trying Tactical Meetings, dominates conversations, or fails to support the Facilitator, it’s unlikely the process will thrive. These meetings shift focus from individuals to the group, which can feel threatening to some. But for those with healthy egos, it’s an opportunity: not a loss of control, but a redistribution of power to improve team outcomes.

Structural Change Isn’t the Goal: This is a built-in limitation since Tactical Meetings are meant to keep operations moving, not to rework how the team or company is structured. When deeper issues arise that suggest a need for governance changes (like role adjustments or restructuring), those belong in a different forum, ideally a Governance Meeting. Tactical Meetings can help surface such needs, but don’t aim to resolve them directly.

Processing All Issues: Because Tactical Meetings are time-boxed, not everything will be addressed in a single session. That’s okay. With practice, teams learn to prioritize and act quickly, resulting in the faster and better processing of issues. Over time teams learn to trust the process and know that the most collectively relevant ones will be handled.

Here are a few key differences (i.e. thoughtful adjustments):

Rethinking Roles In Holacracy, roles are clearly defined and fluid, making it easier for people to act in context rather than from hierarchy. In more traditional settings, people often cling to titles like “Team Lead” or “CEO,” which can box them in. Still, I’ve found that the structure and flow of Tactical Meetings helps keep conversations focused, even when roles aren’t fully formalized.

Do We Still Need a Secretary? In classic Holacracy, the Secretary (or “Scribe,” as I prefer) supports the meeting by documenting key actions, freeing the Facilitator to guide the process. However, with ANYbotics not operating in a role-based manner, this in-meeting role felt unnatural. Instead, we used shared tools that allowed everyone to take part in live note-taking. The result? Everyone stayed engaged, and action items were captured organically. No dedicated Secretary was required.

Final Thoughts

Tactical Meetings aren't magic, but they can feel magical when done right. They reduce friction, foster inclusion, and give structure without bureaucracy. Whether you’re leading a product team, a sales unit, or the executive floor, try some rounds of Tactical Meetings. See what shifts. See who speaks up. See who makes space for others. See what can be achieved.

I hope that this article has already enlightened you in some meaningful way. I’d love to hear how you implement or adapt this format. What tweaks worked for you? What resistance did you encounter? Let’s share and evolve this together.

Additional Resources

  • How To Run Effective Meetings - The Holacracy Way
  • Tactical Meetings in the Holacracy Constitution

item.title: My Journey Beyond Numbers to Humanity in Leadership
item.description: In the middle of a mass layoff, I saw a way out that the spreadsheet couldn't show me. It cost me a job I loved.
item.content:encoded:
In the middle of a mass layoff, I saw a way out that the spreadsheet couldn't show me. It cost me a job I loved.

That moment is the clearest example I have of what I call rehumanizing the numbers, an ability that I believe separates good managers from great executive leaders. Let me explain the concept first, then tell you the story.

Two Stages of Leadership Most People Already Know

Stage One: Leading from Instinct

My leadership journey started young. At 17, I was promoted to restaurant manager at a Taco Bell in Canada while still in high school. My leadership was entirely instinct-driven: motivate the crew, hold the team together under pressure, celebrate the wins. Numbers were something that happened somewhere else. Leadership and data felt like entirely separate worlds.

Stage Two: Learning to Lead with Numbers

As I gained global experience, I realized that effective management requires breaking down an organization into numbers. This means stripping away emotion (at least temporarily) to assess financial and operational health objectively. This step is like (temporarily) removing the human from the equation if the human was ever part of the equation. Data-driven decision-making is not new and is essential, but it can go too far when leaders hide behind numbers, waiting for perfect data or using them as a shield to avoid tough calls.

One of my favorite executive exercises is determining whether an organization can genuinely afford its next initiative. Done well, this analysis ties together resource planning, roadmapping, cash flow, and portfolio management into a coherent picture. I've seen organizations resist this kind of analysis, forcing initiatives into existence on emotional conviction rather than organizational feasibility. I've worked with CFOs who championed this transparency and others who actively resisted it. When the analysis was available, some leadership teams changed course intelligently. Others ignored it, often to the organization's cost.

Too many leaders stop here. This makes sense since the ability to break down complex systems into numbers is enormously powerful and essentially infinite in its application. It feels like mastery.

Yet, I know that there is another level.

Stage Three: Rehumanizing the Numbers

In my view, the transformation from a “good manager” to a “great (executive) leader” lies in the ability to rehumanize those numbers. Once you analyze the numbers, everyone profits from reconnecting the numbers to the people behind them before taking action. Great leaders understand that every figure represents real individuals with aspirations, challenges, and families.

Consider layoffs. Instead of executing them as a cold, financial necessity, a great leader is ready to take risks for their people and organization. Can we offer better severance, career counselling, or thoughtfully help them transition to new internal or external opportunities?

When done well and with courage in times of crisis, rehumanizing numbers might even reveal bold opportunities, like investing in upskilling (e.g. teaching your workforce to embrace and work with AI automation to elevate their work), or creatively expanding the organization in a downturn instead of retreating. By doing so, you not only mitigate the negative impact but also demonstrate compassion and respect for your team, potentially advancing the organization instead of only protecting the numbers.

A Personal Story: Alternative Solution to Achieving 40% Cuts

At one of my former companies, a financial crisis struck just as we were growing. Instead of assessing each company’s unique situation, our new Silicon Valley investors imposed a blanket directive: reduce workforce costs by 40%.

Although our European-based company could have explored mechanisms like furlough programs that could buffer the crisis, the founders fully embraced the investors’ orders, to my surprise. Rational discussions about alternatives failed. The task of executing these drastic cuts fell largely to me as the overall R&D leader.

I created different business cases: a -40% scenario, a -10% “trim the fat” approach, and even a +10% growth plan to capitalize on new market opportunities. The founders refused to budge. Ultimately, it was their company, but I feared it would never recover from the loss of talent. According to those who stayed, it still hasn’t.

Forced to study the -40% scenario in more detail and prepare for its execution, I began to see the people behind the numbers:

  • One employee was financially supporting his extended family.
  • Another, living in a conservative country, had privately shared his sexual orientation with only a few trusted colleagues.
  • One was a personal friend and neighbour.
  • Another just left a company to join ours.

All of them were effective, well-performing team members.

Then I began to see a difficult new option as I continued combining the numbers and the human element. Our company was a highly distributed organization across the globe and many of the names on the long list earned very well for their countries, but their cost to the organization was relatively low and was a fraction of my Swiss-based compensation. I realized that around six international positions could be saved if I left. I loved my job, was high performing and didn’t want to go. However, I took confidence in the belief that I could find work easier in this period of crisis. So, perhaps quicker than I should have, I communicated my proposal to the CEO (i.e. If it must be -40%, then I go, they stay) under the condition that these people keep their jobs.

To my heartbreak, the CEO accepted, yet it was relieving to know that multiple team members would keep their jobs.

While this wasn’t the first time that I had rehumanized numbers, it was an important time. So, I kept it a priority to apply a strong human touch during the execution of this mass termination. This included a range of measures like:

  • Establishing a support channel via chat and private email so that all who chose to join could clarify their situation, support others, and be supported
  • Investing extra energy in final references that could stand out from the standard writing

Soon after leaving this company I found exciting new work and my career continued.

In hindsight, I would have changed the hastiness of my decision, but ultimately, I would make the same decision again. Years later, I still find relief and satisfaction that I found an alternative solution beyond the numbers in such a moment of crisis. It still feels right today.

Beyond the Data: Leading with Humanity

The outcome of rehumanizing numbers should rarely be so personal. This was an extreme case. Most of the time, it means smaller things: the conversation before the decision, the severance package you fight for, the reference letter you actually mean.

But the principle holds at every scale and I hope that my story inspires a few more leaders to continue their leadership journey into more humanity.

Rehumanizing numbers isn’t about avoiding tough decisions. It’s about making better ones! Great leaders rehumanize the numbers, ensuring that every decision reflects compassion, empathy, and a commitment to the well-being of their team and/or greater organization.

While not easy, leaders who master both numbers and humanity create organizations that are not only efficient but also resilient, trusted, and ultimately more successful.

Such leaders must be celebrated.

Throughout my career, I’ve actively applied and coached the concept of rehumanizing numbers. Most recently, I did so over 4.5 years as CTO Solutions/CPO at ANYbotics (embodied AI, autonomous mobile robotics).

Originally published in the Technology Company Leadership newsletter on LinkedIn on 17 March 2025. Read it on LinkedIn.
